speaker: The Announcer
text: Previously, on LAiDIES: our heroine stopped feeling behind, and finally stopped putting it off — one avoided email, nine seconds flat, and the realization that AI is just the most talented new hire she'll ever manage.

speaker: The Announcer
text: And on this episode: she types something vague into the machine, gets back a paragraph of absolutely nothing... and learns that talking to AI isn't coding — it's delegation.

speaker: The Announcer
text: This is Episode Two: Tell Me What You Want.

speaker: The Heroine
text: It's nine-fifteen on a Tuesday, and I am losing a staring contest with a paragraph.

speaker: The Heroine
text: I'd asked one of the AI tools to draft talking points for a meeting, and what it gave back is... technically words.

speaker: The Heroine
text: "Leverage synergies." "Drive alignment." "Circle back to maximize stakeholder buy-in." It reads like a motivational poster that went to business school and came back worse.

speaker: The Heroine
text: And the maddening part?

speaker: The Heroine
text: Yesterday, the same tool wrote me a project update for my director that I barely had to touch.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Same app.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Same me.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Same tragic office lighting.

speaker: The Heroine
text: One day it reads my mind, and the next it hands me a throw pillow.

speaker: The Heroine
text: And I couldn't help but wonder... why does AI read my mind some days, and completely ignore me on others?

speaker: The Heroine
text: Welcome back to LAiDIES — smart, busy women learning AI one Wednesday at a time, from a little internet town called SUNNYVAiLE.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Last week, for your try-on, you held auditions: one task, all three tools, just to see how differently they each answer.

speaker: The Heroine
text: So you already know the tool has opinions.

speaker: The Heroine
text: This week is your half of the conversation — the ask itself.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Because it turns out that matters even more than which tool you pick.

speaker: The Heroine
text: So I did what I do with any problem I can't out-stubborn at my desk: I took it to town.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Corner table at the Blend and Snap, oat latte, K-S-V-L on low.

speaker: The Heroine
text: And I pulled them both back up — the word-salad talking points from that morning, and the director update I'd barely had to touch the day before — and set them side by side.

speaker: The Heroine
text: It wasn't the tool that changed between the two.

speaker: The Heroine
text: It was me: what I'd typed to get each one.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Because here's the punchline, and it took me an embarrassingly long time to see it: AI can't read your mind.

speaker: The Heroine
text: What's in your head stays in your head... until you type it out.

speaker: The Heroine
text: And that word everyone throws around — prompt?

speaker: The Heroine
text: The computer nerds didn't even invent it.

speaker: The Heroine
text: They lifted it from the theater kids.

speaker: The Heroine
text: The two lunch tables that never once overlapped — and the AV club quietly swiped 'prompt' right off the drama club.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Think about your coffee order.

speaker: The Heroine
text: At your regular spot, you barely have to say it — they know your usual, because you built that over a hundred Tuesdays.

speaker: The Heroine
text: But AI is not your regular spot.

speaker: The Heroine
text: It's the brand-new café across town, and if you breeze in and say "the usual," you get a blank look — or a plain drip going cold on the counter, which you can't even be mad about, because you never told the barista what you actually wanted to drink.

speaker: The Heroine
text: And the AI isn't holding out on you — it genuinely can't see what you didn't say.

speaker: The Heroine
text: It has your words, and nothing else.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Not your job, not who's going to read this, not the meeting sitting on your calendar.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Every detail you leave in your head is one it's forced to guess at.

speaker: The Heroine
text: So you spell it out — every time — and the guessing stops.

speaker: The Heroine
text: That's prompting.

speaker: The Heroine
text: So how long until it knows your order by heart, like your regular spot does?

speaker: The Heroine
text: Right now — it doesn't.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Every new chat, you walk into the café a stranger again.

speaker: The Heroine
text: But you can teach it to remember you — your usual, your voice, the way you like things — so you stop starting from zero.

speaker: The Heroine
text: That's an episode of its own, and we'll get there.

speaker: The Heroine
text: For today: assume it forgot, and tell it again.

speaker: The Heroine
text: The Spice Girls had this figured out decades ago. (Wait...

speaker: The Heroine
text: Decades?

speaker: The Heroine
text: Ooff.

speaker: The Heroine
text: That is a jagged little pill to swallow, isn't it...) "Tell me what you want, what you really, really want." Those iconic lyrics from the Spice Girls were not gesturing at a vibe.

speaker: The Heroine
text: They wanted specifics.

speaker: The Heroine
text: AI is exactly the same.

speaker: The Heroine
text: It will zig-a-zig-ah all day long — but it only does useful work when you tell it precisely what you need.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Which is why the patron saint of this episode is David Rose.

speaker: The Heroine
text: I know, I know.

speaker: The Heroine
text: You're thinking, "But he's not from the nineties, or the two-thousands?" And you're right.

speaker: The Heroine
text: But he is so fabulous that we just had to make one exception.

speaker: The Heroine
text: In the immortal words of Shakespeare: A Rose by any other name...

speaker: The Heroine
text: If you've seen Schitt's Creek, you know David is pathologically specific — the wine, the sweater, the exact drape of the sweater.

speaker: The Heroine
text: And you remember Moira telling him to "fold in the cheese," and him standing in that kitchen screaming, "WHAT DOES THAT MEAN?!" That is your AI, every single time you type "write me an email about the project." It is trying.

speaker: The Heroine
text: But you handed it "fold in the cheese" — when what it needed was "scrape the spatula along the bottom of the bowl, lift, turn it over, turn the bowl, and repeat." And yes, full confession: I had AI write that cooking description for me, because I do not cook. (Oh, and P-S-A: if you haven't seen Schitt's Creek, what are you even doing with your life?

speaker: The Heroine
text: Get on it!)

speaker: The Heroine
text: Ok, back to what I did.

speaker: The Heroine
text: The fix, it turned out, was something I already knew how to do.

speaker: The Heroine
text: I stopped typing at AI like a Google search — three vague words, fingers crossed — and I started briefing it like a smart new hire in her first week.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Who is this for?

speaker: The Heroine
text: What do they care about?

speaker: The Heroine
text: What's the tone?

speaker: The Heroine
text: How long?

speaker: The Heroine
text: What should it absolutely not include?

speaker: The Heroine
text: Have we done one of these before that she can copy from?

speaker: The Heroine
text: Every one of those is a question you already ask when you hand work to a person.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Prompting isn't technical.

speaker: The Heroine
text: It's delegation.

speaker: The Heroine
text: I even put those on a card for your study pack — a handful of questions, thirty seconds, and your ask stops being a shrug and starts being an instruction.

speaker: The Heroine
text: But if you only ever steal one, steal the last: show it an example.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Paste in one you already love — an email that landed, a summary that worked — and say "match this." Nothing gets you a better answer faster than handing it something to copy.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Let me show you, because the difference is almost rude.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Say you've got a twelve-page policy change to get in front of a meeting.

speaker: The Heroine
text: The lazy ask — what you'd type without LAiDIES — is just: "summarize this policy change for my stakeholders." And back comes... everything.

speaker: The Heroine
text: A wall of text — accurate, thorough, and completely useless in the two minutes you've got.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Background, rationale, timelines, exemptions, appendices A through D — all weighted exactly the same, because it can't tell what matters to you from what doesn't.

speaker: The Heroine
text: It's Ross, screaming "PIVOT" — technically a direction, zero help getting the couch up the stairs.

speaker: The Heroine
text: You still have to do the reading.

speaker: The Heroine
text: So you try it again — only this time you brief it out loud, the way you'd brief a person.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Something like: "Summarize this for six senior managers who have two minutes before a meeting.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Tell them what's changing, when it takes effect, what their teams actually do differently, and whether it touches budget.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Cut the backstory.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Bullets — about a hundred and fifty words.

speaker: The Heroine
text: And here's last quarter's summary that landed — match it." And this time, back comes something you would actually send: a subject line, then a handful of tight bullets, in exactly the shape you asked for.

speaker: The Heroine
text: And buried in one of them — a line you would never have caught skimming twelve pages in two minutes: contractors are exempt until the new year, so your vendor team is on a different clock.

speaker: The Heroine
text: That one line is the whole reason you opened AI.

speaker: The Heroine
text: You could have written the summary yourself — what you could not have done, not in the twenty minutes before the meeting, was read twelve pages of compliance language and catch the one exemption that would have blown the whole thing up.

speaker: The Heroine
text: That's not a writing job; it's a reading job — and AI just did it, tailored to exactly what you asked for.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Ninety seconds to write, forty-five to check — forward it without touching a word.

speaker: The Heroine
text: A full "It's Britney, bitch" moment — that unbothered confidence of asking for exactly what you wanted, and getting exactly what you needed.

speaker: The Heroine
text: And if the first answer isn't quite right?

speaker: The Heroine
text: You don't start from scratch — you tell it what's off, exactly like you would with a real new hire.

speaker: The Heroine
text: It's calling into the radio and asking for exactly the song you want to hear (or finally shelling out twenty bucks at H-M-V for the CD), not spinning the dial, hoping it lands on one you like.

speaker: The Heroine
text: And if a voice in your head is going "briefing, context, knowing what to cut — that sounds a little soft to be a real skill" — hold that thought.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Because later that week I went looking, at the LIBRAiRY in town, the reference desk where you go to actually look things up — and I found the proof.

speaker: The Heroine
text: A study, Harvard and BCG, over seven hundred consultants.

speaker: The Heroine
text: On the right kind of task, the ones using AI worked about twenty-five percent faster and turned out work rated roughly forty percent higher in quality.

speaker: The Heroine
text: But the thing that separated the winners was not technical.

speaker: The Heroine
text: It was knowing how to brief, how to hand over context, when to push back.

speaker: The Heroine
text: And the best line about it comes from someone who co-authored that very study — Ethan Mollick, a Wharton professor and one of the most-read, most-trusted voices on actually using AI.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Here's what he said:

speaker: The Expert
text: The skills that are so often dismissed as soft turned out to be the hard ones.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Which means the woman who writes a thorough project brief — who thinks about her reader, spells out exactly what she needs, knows what to cut — is already ahead of the guy who types three words and expects the machine to read his mind.

speaker: The Heroine
text: And here's the part worth sitting with.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Communicating clearly.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Thinking critically.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Reading what a person actually needs.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Those got filed under "soft skills" for a generation — soft, as in nice-to-have, as in not the real work.

speaker: The Heroine
text: The consolation prize.

speaker: The Heroine
text: But study after study now lands in the same place: in the age of AI, those are the skills that separate the people who win.

speaker: The Heroine
text: And not instead of the hard skills — on top of them.

speaker: The Heroine
text: So if you're a sharp communicator with real judgment who also knows her stuff — that was never the soft skill set.

speaker: The Heroine
text: That's the one that wins.

speaker: The Heroine
text: And it's exactly what makes this thing work for you.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Which brings me to my favourite part of every episode.

speaker: The Heroine
text: We call it the cocktail party explanation — the line you can actually say out loud at happy hour when someone asks, "so, what's a prompt, really?" Here it is: a prompt isn't code.

speaker: The Heroine
text: It's a delegation.

speaker: The Heroine
text: You're not programming a machine — you're briefing an assistant.

speaker: The Heroine
text: And you already know how to brief.

speaker: The Heroine
text: You have been doing it your whole career, for people who needed clearer instructions.

speaker: The Heroine
text: This one is just faster, never sleeps, and will absolutely fold the cheese wrong if you don't tell her how.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Oh — and the first person I tried that line on?

speaker: The Heroine
text: A friend who's been "meaning to get to this" for about a year.

speaker: The Heroine
text: She got it in one sentence.

speaker: The Heroine
text: So on my way out of town, I stopped by the Post Office and mailed her a postcard — the kind you send from a place you actually love — and wrote on the back: because SUNNYVAiLE is even better with your people in it.

speaker: The Heroine
text: And... that's the episode.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Now — your try-on.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Ten minutes, not homework, and everything you need lives at laidies.ai.

speaker: The Heroine
text: That's "LAiDIES" spelled with an i in the middle: L, A, i, D, I, E, S.

speaker: The Heroine
text: And if you'd rather read than listen — or you want to see that before-and-after with your own eyes — the whole episode's written up there too, laid out side by side.

speaker: The Heroine
text: This week: hand one real task to an AI tool twice.

speaker: The Heroine
text: First the lazy way — three vague words, the way you'd Google it.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Then the David Rose way: who it's for, what they care about, the tone, the length, and what to leave out.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Put the two answers side by side.

speaker: The Heroine
text: The difference isn't the tool getting smarter between tries.

speaker: The Heroine
text: It's you getting specific.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Then, if you're feeling it: grab this week's study pack at the Blend and Snap, take the pop quiz at SUNNYVAiLE High — ten questions, plus two bonus, banking butterfly clips in your closet — and turn on K-S-V-L, ninety-nine point nine, for this week's anthem — do not skip it.

speaker: The Heroine
text: It's this week's lesson, in platform sandals.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Don't just learn from books; learn from hooks.

speaker: The Heroine
text: And if this is your first Wednesday with us, stop by Makeover on Main for your residence card.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Two minutes, free, and everything you collect starts counting.

speaker: The Heroine
text: So remember, LAiDIES: AI can't read your mind — so tell it what you want... what you really, really want.

speaker: The Heroine
text: See you next Wednesday... in SUNNYVAiLE.

speaker: The Announcer
text: Next time on LAiDIES: the machine hands our heroine a beautiful, confident answer — with one small detail that could blow up the whole meeting.

speaker: The Announcer
text: Come back next week for Episode Three: The Burn Book Problem.
